body.text: With Victoria's state election just around the corner on November 28, political parties are ramping up their promises to voters.
To help you keep up, we will be updating this story with some of the key pledges from the Labor government and Liberal-National opposition, as well as the priorities of One Nation and the Greens.
We're drawing on party announcements and the list being kept by Victoria's independent Parliamentary Budget Office, which you can see on its website in full.
As you will see, many of the government's commitments that extend into the next few years were unveiled in the state budget.
The Coalition has been rolling out a raft of more specific commitments as the campaign heats up.
Crime and justice
Rising community concern over crime has formed a cornerstone of election campaigns for the major parties.
Here's what's being promised:
Labor

Labor has promised to swell the ranks of Victoria Police, recruiting 1,500 officers and opening a second police academy at Wyndham in Melbourne's west. Police numbers would also be boosted via a $62-million investment to recruit up to 200 reservists for desk duties.

If re-elected, Labor said it would increase jail sentences for offenders convicted of serious sexual offences, with maximum sentences of life for rape, and a standard sentence of 30 years for the murder of a partner.

The Carroll government has pledged to tackle organised crime with a new $170 million permanent unit. Some $66.5 million would also be invested in providing new technology for police, including tools to tackle cybercrime.

Labor has committed $10 million towards a Local Community Safety Infrastructure Fund for councils to buy CCTV and improved lighting, and $10 million for a Hospitality Security Fund to allow eligible venues to upgrade their security systems.
Coalition
The Coalition has promised an even heavier investment in Victoria Police, pledging to reopen more than 40 police stations across the state and recruit an additional 3,000 officers to help staff them.

The hiring drive would also extend to Protective Services Officers (PSOs), with the Coalition promising to recruit 200 PSOs to patrol train stations, and a further 200 to patrol high-risk shopping centres and precincts.
The opposition said it would introduce new laws based on the United States' RICO Act to target the leaders of organised crime.
The bail system would be reformed under a Coalition government with a one-strike rule introduced for offenders committing crimes while on bail.
The Coalition would expand adult sentencing provisions for youths to cover 20 serious offences including arson, home invasions and carjacking.
To address youth crime, it has also pledged to invest $100 million in early intervention and rehabilitation programs.
The opposition would also outlaw coercive control, and introduce UK-style domestic violence disclosure laws.
Greens

The Greens are pushing for a $1 billion investment into a new Office of Community Safety and Crime Prevention, mirroring a policy introduced in New York City. The investment would go towards crime prevention, early intervention and diversion programs and 24/7 crisis outreach teams.
The Greens are also campaigning on repealing changes the government made to strengthen bail laws in 2025.
The party is fighting to raise the age of criminal responsibility to 14 and eliminate life sentences for children.
It also wants to ban the police use of sniffer dogs for drug detection, and decriminalise personal use and possession of drugs in small quantities.
One Nation

One Nation's policing policy would boost police numbers by offering sign-on bonuses for armed forces members, veterans and police officers from interstate and other English speaking countries. Accommodation allowances and on-call mental health support to police would be provided under One Nation's policy.

Under its proposed legal changes, children charged with a serious violent offence would be charged as adults, with the age of criminal responsibility returned to 10 years old. Parents would also be responsible for fines or damage caused by their children.

One Nation has outlined plans for greater investment in the court system, building three new Magistrates' Courts at Melton, Epping and Pakenham, increasing the number of active magistrates to 170 and doubling the number of judicial registrars from 18 to 36. It has also pledged additional funding for the Office of Public Prosecutions.
Under One Nation's reforms, a 24/7 bail court would be established, and a presumption against bail would be created for repeat offenders and those committing an offence while already on bail.
One Nation also promised to introduce UK-style self-defence in the home laws, and introduce a trial to legalise OC (capsicum) spray.
Health

The election approaches amid protracted pay bargaining negotiations between the government and doctors and allied health professionals, with the medical sector calling for better staff conditions and greater funding.
Here's what each party is pledging on health:
Labor

Labor has made free dental the core of its election campaign on health. The Carroll government has promised to invest $230 million in 10 free public dental clinics across the state, with seven in Melbourne and three in regional Victoria.

The government would also spend $277 million on opening the new emergency department at Werribee Mercy Hospital, expanding the Angliss Hospital and Pakenham Community Hospital, and boosting performance at University Hospital Geelong, and hospitals in Craigieburn, Cranbourne and Mernda.

The Thomas Embling forensic mental health hospital would also receive a $125 million funding boost, while hospitals in Melbourne's west would receive $240.5 million to expand maternity delivery services with 32 new post-natal beds.
The Carroll government has pledged a $53.6 million boost to the Victorian Patient Transport Assistance Scheme, providing more funding for regional and rural Victorians travelling for medical care.
Labor has also pledged to make abortion care free if re-elected.
Coalition
The Coalition has focused its campaign efforts on cutting surgery wait times at Victorian hospitals.

It has pledged $1.27 billion towards cutting the waitlist for elective surgeries, promising to deliver an extra 25,000 procedures a year, while also guaranteeing $99 million towards patient transit lounges in hospitals.

Regional Victorians have been promised major health investments, with $850 million pledged for a West Gippsland Hospital in Drouin East, $350 million pledged towards Wonthaggi Hospital, $180 million to upgrade Mildura Base Public Hospital, $100 million for Albury Wodonga Health and $45 million for Hamilton Base Hospital.

The opposition has also promised to build a new youth mental health facility in Parkville, offering $5 million to begin planning it, and has matched a Labor promise to make abortion care free if elected.
Greens

The Greens have pledged to fight to save health promotion agency VicHealth and introduce a policy mandating that 5 per cent of the current health budget is put towards prevention and health promotions. A further 3 per cent would be mandated spending on community health services.
The Greens have promised to invest $3 billion to open 20 publicly owned dental clinics and make dental care free for all Victorians.

If elected, the Greens would use influence in the next parliament to fight for $15 million towards providing greater access to abortion services and $10 million towards more publicly funded homebirth programs. The party's platform also calls for free and comprehensive abortion and contraceptive care to all Victorians.
It is campaigning on a drug harm-reduction platform, promising to legalise cannabis, expand legal pill testing and expand access to medically supervised injecting rooms.
One Nation
One Nation has pledged to cut down on hospital administration and invest in more doctors and nurses with guarantees on minimum services and 24/7 emergency departments in regional areas.
The party's platform also calls for the introduction of nurse-led discharging and prescribing to increase patient flow, mirroring policies currently in effect in other Australian states.

It is calling for $136 million towards a families funding package, providing one-off payments to expectant mothers who choose private care, and fully funding out-of-pocket costs for those in the public system.

One Nation wants to abolish standalone DEI (Diversity, Equity, Inclusion) and ESG (Environment, Social, Governance) programs that do not demonstrate a necessary purpose and invest savings into frontline care.
The party said it would also seek to standardise electronic medical record systems across the state and make them interoperable.
One Nation said it does not plan to change abortion laws in the state.
Roads
The condition of Victoria's roads and the number of potholes around the state has been a major talking point on the campaign trail this year.
Here's what each party is promising to do if elected:
Labor

Labor has pledged to double the number of potholes fixed this year from 250,000 to 500,000 with a $352 million investment, while also piloting a program to have minimum-security prisoners perform roadside maintenance.
Billions have also been promised for major upgrades to roads and intersections in Melbourne's outer-suburbs.

The government would invest a further $550 million to upgrade the Western Freeway between Melton and Caroline Springs, $494 million to upgrade Somerton Road in Greenvale, $350 million to duplicate Hallam Road in Hallam and Hampton Park, $270 million to upgrade Findon Road in Epping, $195 million to widen Point Cook Road in Seabrook, $180 million to widen Evans Road in Cranbourne West, $170 million to widen Taylors Road in Kings Park, $90 million to replace a roundabout with traffic lights in Hoppers Crossing and $83 million to upgrade roads in Wyndham Vale.
Nearly $49 million would also be invested in motorcycle safety, introducing barriers and surface upgrades in parts of the state and strengthening the motorcycle licensing scheme.
Coalition
The Coalition has promised to boost current spending on road maintenance by 25 per cent, pledging $5 billion to repair Victoria's roads.
The opposition said it would fix one million potholes and establish a new government body to handle the repairs.
Victoria's 48 regional councils have been promised $288 million to fix local roads and bridges at their own discretion.
The Coalition has also promised $524 million to duplicate Donnybrook Road between Woodstock and Kalkallo, where residents have told the ABC traffic is at a standstill during rush hour.
Another $607 million would be spent on duplicating Thompsons Road between Clyde North and Officer South.
Greens
The Greens have proposed bringing VicRoads back into government hands, diverting money saved into fixing the state's roads.
Five per cent of the existing transport budget would be dedicated to a network of safe bike routes across Melbourne and regional centres under the Greens.

The party will also seek to introduce 30kph speed limits in residential areas, extend truck bans in residential areas of Kensington, North Melbourne and West Melbourne, and double registration fees for vehicles with bonnets over 120cm wide.
One Nation
One Nation has promised to publish the condition and funding of every major regional road and create a public pothole portal for Victorians to make reports.
The party has pledged to lock in ongoing funding for regional roads and fix the state's maintenance backlog.
Housing
Here's what each party is pledging for housing:
Labor

Labor has committed to building 26,500 new homes and reserving them for first home buyers at market prices. The homes would be built across Melbourne and major regional cities, with the first homes expected in 2027.
It has a longer-term plan of building more than 300,000 new homes by 2051 with its promised Activity Centres, which would see high-rise apartments of up to 20 stories built in inner-city suburbs.
Labor has also committed to redeveloping the cohealth site in Collingwood, delivering 69 new social homes along with renovating the health service.
The party has promised to roll back changes it made to land tax, progressively dropping it back to previous levels over the course of six years.
Coalition
The Coalition has promised to axe Labor's proposed Activity Centres if elected, and said it would give locals greater voice in the planning system.
The opposition has pledged to expand Melbourne's Capital City Zone to Fishermans Bend, North Melbourne, Fitzroy and Collingwood to allow for more homes in inner Melbourne.
The Coalition would also reverse Labor's increases to land tax, promising to reverse the threshold for land tax to 2023 levels.
Greens

The Greens are advocating for $4 billion to be spent building 88,000 new public homes and upgrading existing public housing. The party would also block the current planned demolition of public housing towers.
The party has vowed to abolish street auctions for home sales, and require every home to be sold at a fixed price.
Stamp duty would be abolished for homes worth less than $1.1 million, and discounted for homes worth less than $1.6 million, under Greens policy.
The Greens have proposed a two-year rent freeze across the state, with a ban on rent increases in the first two years of every new tenancy. Rent rises would also be tied to wage growth or inflation.
The party's policy platform allocates $50 million towards establishing an independent rental regulator with a landlord licensing scheme.
One Nation
One Nation's policy platform includes a review of every government fee, tax and charge related to the cost of a new home and cut ones no longer justified.
The party said it would raise the foreign purchaser duty on residential properties in Victoria.
It has pledged to free up granny flats and the rental of spare rooms without state interference, and mandate community consultation before high-rise development in established suburbs.
It said it planned to provide incentives for private and community organisations to deliver more low-cost housing and free up under-used government land for housing.
Transport
The Suburban Rail Loop has dominated the election campaigns of both major parties, with its significant cost becoming a policy battleground for Labor and the Coalition.
Here's what the major parties are promising on transport:
Labor

The Carroll government has committed to building the Suburban Rail Loop, but has promised to slash $1 billion from its budget by removing additions such as car parking at stations and pedestrian bridges.
It has also promised to commission an independent review to claw back another $1 billion in savings to bring the total estimated cost of the project to $32.3 billion.
Labor would spend $673.6 million to build 25 more X'Trapolis 2.0 trains, retiring older trains on the Craigieburn and Upfield lines.
Labor has also pledged to fund a $80 million study to investigate and plan the duplication of the Upfield Line.
Coalition
The Coalition said it would pause and review the Suburban Rail Loop if elected.
It has promised to invest $1.7 billion in 25 new hybrid electric trains on the Melton and Wyndham Vale lines.
The trains they would replace would be reallocated to regional Victoria to boost capacity during peak times.
Greens
The Greens are calling for all public transport to be made permanently free, and have trams and trains run at least every 10 minutes from 7am to 10pm.
The party supports the construction of a second Melbourne Metro tunnel, reconfiguring the City Loop, electrifying the Melton line and fixing the Altona Loop.
It is pushing for $270 million to be spent upgrading the state's bus system, $245 million to run regional trains and coaches more often, and $225 million to build accessible tram stops.
One Nation
One Nation will push to cancel the Suburban Rail Loop project altogether.
Instead, the party said it would like to redirect funds to other infrastructure projects, including electrifying the Melton Line and completing the Airport Rail Link.
Education
School funding remains a hot button issue in the education state.

Premier Ben Carroll served as the education minister before rising to the top job, and oversaw protracted negotiations over teacher pay earlier this year. More recently, he signed Victoria up to providing its share of schools funding recommended in the Gonski report.
Now, the parties are pledging millions more towards schools in a bid to win over voters.
Here are what the parties have promised for the education sector:
Labor

Schools in Melbourne's north-west would receive a funding boost with $10.73 million committed to building a performing arts centre at Keilor Downs College, and $19.74 million to upgrade The Grange P-12 College in Hoppers Crossing.

Labor has committed $222.2 million to reforming the Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority, following production mistakes in recent years allowing high school students to access answers to their exams.
The Carroll government has pledged $59.4 million towards funding free school uniforms and school breakfasts for families under financial strain.
Labor has also promised to delivery the state's first publicly-owned apprenticeship academy, offering 2,000 electrical trade apprenticeships over the next four years.
Coalition
The Coalition has pledged to build three new select-entry high schools, and transition six existing government schools to select or partial-select entry.
The opposition has committed $222 million towards building 10 new technical schools across the state, educating up to 5,000 students.
It would also direct $115 million towards a fund that would cover half the off-the-job training costs for Victorian apprentices.
It has also promised to introduce reforms to address classroom behaviour at Victorian schools, and review the curriculum to reduce teacher workloads.
Greens
The Greens have backed a policy to make public schools completely free by ending requests for voluntary contributions from parents.

The party said it would fight to make university free, and pledged to review the eight public university acts in Victoria. The Greens said it would ensure students and teachers were on university councils and introduce a cap on vice-chancellor salaries.
The Greens have backed embedding First Nations frameworks in early childhood education and exploring introducing anti-racism, social cohesion and inclusion programs into the Victorian curriculum.
One Nation
One Nation's policy calls for the replacement of the current Victorian curriculum with "a clear, sequenced, knowledge-rich syllabus" prioritising literacy, numeracy, science, history and civics.
The party has proposed introducing a school vouchers system to allow families to choose between schools.
One Nation said it would expand dedicated trade schools while also making it easier for communities to establish independent, specialist and alternative schools.
Environment, energy and climate

The Victoria to New South Wales Interconnector West (VNI West) high-voltage transmission line project has become a hot-button issue in the state's west, prompting anger from local farming communities. The issue has split the major parties, with the future of the project hinging on the election.
Here's what each party is pledging for the environment, energy and climate:
Labor
Labor has committed Victoria to an emissions target of net zero by 2045 and is rolling out transmission projects aimed at connecting renewable power generated in the state's west to the power grid.
But Premier Ben Carroll has announced an independent review of the cost of one of those projects, the Western Renewables Link.

The Carroll government has pledged to create a dedicated mineral resources royalties fund if re-elected, with $500 million to be raised over four years. All of the proceeds would be directed towards regional Victoria.
Labor has promised to introduce a 2km buffer zone between new waste-to-energy facilities and existing homes.
Coalition
The Coalition has "no plans" to change the legislation setting down Victoria's target of net-zero emissions by 2045, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has said.
But it has flagged major changes to two of Labor's key renewable energy infrastructure projects.
The Coalition said it would cancel Labor's VNI West transmission project and halt the Western Renewables Link, pending a review.
It has promised to reintroduce a 2km buffer zone around wind turbines to prevent them being built close to homes.
The opposition has also pledged to repeal Labor's ban on gas in homes, and open the doors to new gas projects in the state.
The Coalition would introduce urban solar parks to encourage solar and battery installations on commercial rooftops.
It said it would also guarantee weekly red bin collection for households and scrap mandates requiring councils to have a fourth separate bin for glass.
Greens
The Greens have pledged to establish a $1 billion climate adaptation and mitigation seed fund for communities affected by climate disasters.
The party has promised to invest $2 billion into the State Electricity Commission to put publicly-owned solar panels on schools, public housing and government buildings.
It has promised a moratorium on all AI data centres and waste-to-energy incineration projects.
It would block on all new fossil fuel projects in the state, including Viva's gas import terminal in Geelong and closing the Loy Yang A power plant in the Latrobe Valley earlier than planned.
The Greens would also ban logging in native forests, duck hunting, and greyhound and jumps racing in Victoria.
One Nation
One Nation has promised to scrap all net-zero targets and subsidies, and repeal Victoria's state ban on nuclear energy.
The party would also cancel VNI West, Western Renewables Link and other large-scale transmission projects.
The ban on gas in homes would be reversed, with support given for commercial offshore gas extraction.

The party said it would ban new data centres and battery storage on agricultural land, and require community consultation and water management plans before approving data centres and batteries near homes.
Duck and deer hunting would be supported under One Nation, and the party said it would pursue eradicating European carp and redfin from the state.
Indigenous affairs

During this election campaign, discussion in Indigenous affairs has been centred around Victoria's historic Treaty agreement. Labor signed Australia's first modern treaty agreement with the country's Indigenous people in 2025. Treaty legislation lead to the creation of the new democratically elected body Gellung Warl.

When members of parliament introduce new bills in Victoria, they are now required to include a statement on how the bill fits with the principles of Treaty and whether the First Peoples' Assembly was consulted. However, Gellung Warl has no powers to veto Victorian policy or legislation.
The government also makes annual payments to the Self Determination Fund, providing about $65 million each year to the fund, which is overseen by Gellung Warl.

The Coalition and One Nation's position of tearing up Treaty has dismayed many Indigenous community leaders, who have argued it would be a backwards step for First Nations people seeking to overcome the disadvantages created by colonisation.
Here's what each political party has pledged moving forward:
Labor
Labor has committed to maintaining Treaty.
It pledged nearly $170 million in this year's budget towards First People's initiatives, which will be spread over the next four years.

The budget includes $7.6 million in funding for a dedicated Koori Hearing List at Melbourne Magistrates' Court to delivery culturally appropriate case management for First Nations accused, and $16 million to build 30 homes as part of a rent-to-buy pilot for First Nations people.
Labor would also allocate $86 million of its $860 million Social Housing Growth Fund to support more First Nations people having access to housing.
Coalition

The Coalition has pledged to repeal the laws underpinning Treaty within its first 100 days in office if elected and move back to a model where policy ideas on Indigenous affairs are managed by a department reporting to a minister.
Parliamentary Budget Office analysis shows the opposition's planned scrapping of Treaty would return roughly $948 million to the budget over a decade from 2025-26 to 2035-36.
The Coalition has also promised $52 million in funding for urgent care pathways through 16 Aboriginal Community Controlled Organisations.
Greens
The Greens strongly support keeping Victoria's Treaty and the signing of further local and statewide treaties.
The party would seek to restructure the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action to make First Nations knowledge and nature protection the primary mandate.
That would be linked to a promised $2 billion seed fund for nature protection, which would support First Nations-led work on protecting and restoring the environment.
It would also entail Traditional Owner management of national and state parks.
One Nation
One Nation backs a policy to scrap the Treaty and abolish Gelling Warl, redirecting its yearly funding to other policies.
Cost of living

Cost-of-living pressures loom as a large issue in this election. According to recent data from Commonwealth Bank, Victoria recorded the equal-slowest annual wage growth in Australia at 3 per cent while national inflation reached 4 per cent in the 12 months to August.
Here's how each party plans to address cost-of-living pressures if elected:
Labor
The Carroll government has promised $30 weekly caps on public transport fares for two years if re-elected.
It has also mirrored a Coalition policy on toll road caps, pledging $191 million towards a $30 weekly toll cap for smaller vehicles.
Labor has also spent much of its re-election campaign highlighting cost of living measures it implemented this year as part of the budget.
These included free and discounted public transport across Victoria until the end of the year, and discounts on car registration until the end of August.
Coalition
The Coalition has said it would address cost-of-living pressures by cutting taxes introduced under Labor, promising no new or increased taxes if elected.
In addition to winding back the land-tax threshold, the Coalition has also committed to repealing several taxes including:
• Payroll taxes on schools
• Taxes on visits to the GP
• Taxes on short-stay accommodation
• The emergency services levy on family homes.
The Coalition said it would also cut payroll taxes and lift the stamp duty-free threshold to $1 million for first home buyers.
It has pledged to review Victoria's tolling system and introduce a $50 weekly toll cap for cars and light commercial vehicles, costed at $90 million a year.
The party said it planned to have Victoria operating a cash surplus, raising more money than it spends, by 2032.
Greens

The Greens party has promised to address cost-of-living pressures through a $500 million investment in vouchers for Victorian households to spend on energy efficient home upgrades such as solar, batteries and insulation.
The party said it would also deliver free energy assessments for renters and offer up to $3,000 off electric cars, e-bikes and two-way chargers.
One Nation
One Nation's policies would cut taxes, repealing Labor increases to land tax and increasing the threshold for payroll tax to make more small employers exempt.
The party said it would also abolish the 10 per cent stamp duty on home, contents and car insurance.
One Nation has also pledged $150 in vouchers for every school-age child in Victoria to be used on sports during the year, as part of a $136 million families funding pledge.
Business

The major parties have promised to strengthen the ties between the government and Victoria's business community. Premier Ben Carroll declared he would reset the relationship between his government and businesses after replacing Jacinta Allan, while Opposition Leader Jess Wilson vowed to declare Victoria re-opened for business if elected.
Here's what each party has planned for Victoria's business sector:
Labor

Labor has promised big changes for pubs, pledging to allow all pubs to trade until 3am and to speed up applications for liquor licences. The party said it would also amend the Food Act 1984 to lift the ban on dogs inside pubs.
The Carroll government would invest $80 million in the Victorian Racing Industry Fund to support horse and greyhound racing.
Coalition
The Coalition would privatise the Melbourne Wholesale Fruit and Vegetable Market at Epping and wind up the Melbourne Market Authority, promising the move will raise $578 million.
It has pledged to standardise local business laws across the state and modernise planning rules for businesses run out of homes.
The party would turn Service Victoria into a singular platform for all business approvals including planning, licensing and registration.
The opposition said it would also establish a Business Approvals Concierge as a single point of contact for businesses to resolve delays and coordinate approvals.
Greens
The Greens will push to trial a four-day working week for the public and private sectors, and implement legislation guaranteeing the right to work from home.
The party also wants to see $100 million go towards providing paid sick leave for casual workers.
The Greens has also pledged to reduce Victorian defence spending to zero, end state contracts for the supply of weapons to United States and Israel, and ban weapons expos from the state.
One Nation
One Nation will use its parliamentary presence to push for tax cuts for small businesses, pledging to remove stamp duty on the establishment of new businesses.
The party has also pledged to lift the payroll tax threshold to make more small employers exempt.
How will each party pay for it?
While each party has made dozens of promises painting their vision for Victoria's future after November 29, the financials behind the promises are less clear.
Here's how each party said it would fund the billions of dollars worth of promises, pledges and guarantees made on the campaign trail:
Labor
Labor said it would deliver $2 billion in savings on the Suburban Rail Loop plan to fund its promises.
It has also pledged to redirect 100 per cent of mineral resources royalties generated by a new fund towards regional Victoria.
Several government bodies including Infrastructure Victoria and Economic Growth Victoria would be wound up, with others such as the Suburban Rail Loop Authority and VIDA being merged.

The Carroll government said it has cut down on spending on consultants and external advisers, saving $70 million. The premier has also instructed ministers to stop spending on non-essential items, such as branded merchandise and apparel for staff.
Coalition

The Coalition said it would save $22 billion over 10 years by instituting a hiring freeze across the public sector and capping the salaries of public service executives. It said the freeze would remain in place until staffing return to 2014/15 levels, adjusted for population.

The opposition said another $10 billion would be saved over 10 years by scrapping Treaty, while a further $1.27 billion in funding for its elective surgery promise would be wholly funded by scrapping government investment fund Breakthrough Victoria.
The Coalition said it will also raise $578 million by privatising the Melbourne Wholesale Fruit and Vegetable Market.
Greens
The Greens party has vowed to try to introduce an ultra-wealth tax for investors owning over $5 million worth of residential properties.
The party said it would raise more than $3 billion a year by introducing a quarterly levy of 0.1 per cent on the big five banks.
Gambling taxes would also increase, with taxes on pokies rising to 75 per cent, online gambling taxes rising to 25 per cent and taxes doubling on casino table games.
One Nation
One Nation said it would fund its election campaign promises by scrapping the Suburban Rail Loop, freeing up the funds for other projects.

It said it would also save money by cutting down on government bureaucracy and introducing a sunset review system for government bodies and entities, which the party said accounted for $35 billion in annual operating expenditure.
It also flagged redirecting funding from Victoria's Treaty.
